risks.description: A condition node's arm count varies 2 to 6+; a layout that assumes 2-3 arms per fork will overflow.
Depth from entry to the furthest node along non-backward edges. A layout that assumes a short chain will need vertical scroll or compression.
An edge whose target sits earlier in reading order than its source. Needs an explicit upward-arrow or back-reference treatment, not a straight-line layout.

A backward edge is not automatically a cycle - only 33 of the 125 backward-edge journeys form an actual cycle (a path that returns to its own source). These need a recursion/traversal guard in the layout algorithm itself; the other 92 are simple back-references and do not.
Multiple named terminal states from one journey. A layout with one exit slot at the bottom fails for these.
Cross-journey and external handoffs on one graph. Each is a link leaving the current view - a layout that treats handoffs like ordinary nodes undercounts how often the reader leaves this journey.
Multiple distinct nodes pointing at the same target node. A tree-shaped layout algorithm cannot represent convergence without either duplicating the node or drawing a shared-target edge.

One node with many outgoing edges (a condition with many branches, or a wait's two arms feeding a further hub). ACQ-10 alone has BOTH the highest fan-in (5) and highest fan-out (8) — the single worst node-density case in the library.

branch.when text (median 60, max 211 chars, see journey-content-stats.json) rendered at a branch point competes for space with the branch arms themselves — this is a layout risk, not just a content-length one, because it happens exactly where the graph is already widest.
risks.threshold: n/a — cross-reference with journey-content-stats.json's branch.when row

note: These candidates overlap heavily with journey-fixture-set.json by design — the same outlier graphs stress both content and layout.
